definition: CycL in computer science and artificial intelligence, is an ontology language used by Douglas Lenat's Cyc artificial intelligence project.
details: Ramanathan V. Guha was instrumental in designing early versions of the language. A close CycL variant exists named MELD. The original version of CycL was a frame language, but the modern version is not. Rather, it is a declarative language based on classical first-order logic, with extensions for modal logic operators and higher-order logic quantification. CycL is used to represent the knowledge stored in the Cyc Knowledge Base, available from Cycorp. The source code written in CycL released with the OpenCyc system is licensed as free and open-source software, to increase its usefulness in supporting the semantic web.

explainer.lead: CycL is a language for writing down facts and rules so a computer can work with knowledge in a precise, logical form. It is used by Douglas Lenat's Cyc project to represent what is stored in the Cyc Knowledge Base.

tiers.eli5: CycL is like a very careful way of writing notes for a computer. Instead of just saving the words "cats are mammals," you write a rule that clearly applies to every cat. The modern language uses logic, although its earliest version organized knowledge in frames.
tiers.practitioner: Use CycL to express declarative facts and rules for the Cyc Knowledge Base rather than as a general-purpose programming language. Modern CycL is based on first-order logic and adds modal operators and higher-order quantification, so treating it as only a frame-and-slot format is misleading. CycL source code released with OpenCyc is free and open-source software, intended in part to support semantic web work.
tiers.paperLevel: Modern CycL is a declarative knowledge-representation language based on classical first-order logic, extended with modal logic operators and higher-order logic quantification. A universal rule has the logical form "for all x, P(x) implies Q(x)," although this is not a statement of CycL's concrete syntax. The original version was a frame language; Ramanathan V. Guha helped design early versions, and MELD is a close variant.

explainer.example: To represent "all cats are mammals," the underlying logical rule is: for every x, if Cat(x), then Mammal(x). Together with Cat(Whiskers), this expresses that Whiskers is a cat and supplies the rule relating cats to mammals.

explainer.intuition: CycL turns human knowledge into explicit statements whose meanings can be expressed through logic. Its job is to describe what is true and what follows from rules, not to specify a sequence of program instructions.
howItWorks: Identify the things, categories, and relationships that the knowledge base must describe.
Write facts and rules declaratively in CycL.
Use first-order logic for the core statements, with modal operators and higher-order quantification where needed.
Store the resulting knowledge in the Cyc Knowledge Base.
explainer.whyItMatters: CycL gives the Cyc project a precise way to represent a large body of knowledge using logic rather than informal prose. Its extensions allow statements beyond plain first-order logic, while the OpenCyc release made some CycL code openly available.
misconceptions: Modern CycL is not a frame language, even though the original version was.
CycL is the representation language, not the Cyc Knowledge Base itself.
MELD is a close variant, not simply another name for CycL.
